This is game 6 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory holds:
- AGENTS.md (4,576 bytes)
- current-position-liberties.js (1,475 bytes)
- game-001.md (2,288 bytes)
- game-001.sgf (316 bytes)

- game-005.sgf (313 bytes)

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

# Game 2 — White versus 12k

Result: Black wins by resignation after B45 J9. White captured one stone; Black captured none before resignation. The 17-stone upper White group was in atari at C8 and could not save itself. Exact record: game-002.sgf (45 board moves; resignation is in RE[B+R]). Chinese area, komi 7, simple ko, no suicide. No engine analysis or sequence-search program was used. Current-position liberty counting was used before every White move.

Progress: the final atari was correctly recognized, unlike game 1. However, counting liberties did not prevent a larger strategic group-safety failure. No demonstrated winning strength at 12k and still no completed scored game.

Opening and shape: White took C3/C6 and expanded through D7/D6/E7/E8. Black's B5–E5 chain separated White's upper and lower groups, while F7/F8 and then F6 restricted the upper group on the right. White's B7/B8/B6 responses to A7/A8/A6 connected the upper stones, but Black A5 joined its edge invasion to the central chain. The invasion was not captured. White's upper group had six liberties after W22 B6, but little enclosed space and no demonstrated two-eye life.

Critical contraction: after W24 E6 B25 F6, the upper group had {B9,C7,C8,D8,E9}. B29 B9 removed B9. W30 C9 created a separate two-liberty group; W32 D9 expanded that group, but B33 C8 invaded the remaining interior. Before W34 D8, the main upper group had {C7,D8,E9}, the C9–D9 pair had {D8,E9}, and Black C8 had {C7,D8}. W34 D8 joined the White groups but left only {C7,E9}; Black C8 was in atari at C7. This was a connection with two liberties and no established eyes, not safety.

White then ran along the first line: W36 E9, W38 F9, W40 G9, W42 H9. Black replied E2, G8, H8, J8. Each White extension still left the large group with just two liberties: C7 and the next point along row 9. This did not produce an escape or eye space. W44 C7 captured Black C8, leaving {C8,J9}. B45 J9 left all 17 stones with {C8}. C8 had four White neighbors, and playing there would fill the group's last liberty without capturing any Black group: suicide. Lessons for game 3:

- Count distinct liberties, then separately check where two eyes or an actual exit can come from. A group with several liberties can already have inadequate living space.
- Before filling an interior liberty to connect, check the merged group's liberties AND remaining eye space. W34 D8 was the clearest warning: two liberties, no established eyes, surrounded externally.
- Do not assume an enemy stone in atari means the surrounding group is safe. Capturing C8 at C7 yielded only one eye point; it could not save the group after the edge was sealed.
- Repeated first-line extensions that keep the same two-liberty count are a danger signal. The F9–H9 chase repeated game 1's edge-trapping error on a larger scale.
- Address shrinking living space earlier. This record does not establish an optimal replacement move; revisit the position before B29 B9 and before filling D8 rather than inventing a proven rescue after the enclosure.

Better future practice: assess liberties and connection routes before an edge attachment; do not repeatedly invest in a chain without a viable exit.

# Game 3 — Black versus 20k

Future practice: assess the territorial balance while developing; repeatedly answering local boundary moves can leave too little elsewhere. This record does not prove an optimal opening replacement.

B35 C5 extended toward White C6/D5. W36 B3 left the three-stone chain with {B4,B5,D3}. It had no established eye space and no clear exit. Recognizing danger only here was too late to establish a rescue in this game.

B37 B5, W38 B6 left {A5,B4,D3}. B39 B4 joined internally but still left only {A4,A5,D3}; it did not improve the liberty count or establish eyes. - Keep the useful outside connections: D3, B2, and G5 joined groups with checked merged liberties while retaining lower interior space.
- Assess area sooner. The connected lower boundary was too small with komi once White secured the top and left. A late risky cut did not solve that strategic deficit.

function inspectLiberties(boardText) {
  const columns = 'ABCDEFGHJ';
  const cells = new Map();
  for (const line of boardText.split('\n')) {
    const m = line.match(/^\s*([1-9])\s+([XO.](?:\s+[XO.]){8})\s+[1-9]\s*$/);
    if (m) m[2].split(/\s+/).forEach((v, x) => cells.set(columns[x] + m[1], v));
  }
  if (cells.size !== 81) throw new Error('Expected a complete 9x9 text board');
  function neighbors(p) {
    const x = columns.indexOf(p[0]), y = Number(p[1]);
    return [[x-1,y],[x+1,y],[x,y-1],[x,y+1]]
      .filter(([a,b]) => a >= 0 && a < 9 && b >= 1 && b <= 9)
      .map(([a,b]) => columns[a]+b);
  }
  const seen = new Set(), groups = [];
  for (const [point, color] of cells) {
    if (color === '.' || seen.has(point)) continue;
    const stones = [], liberties = new Set(), stack = [point];
    seen.add(point);
    while (stack.length) {
      const p = stack.pop(); stones.push(p);
      for (const q of neighbors(p)) {
        if (cells.get(q) === '.') liberties.add(q);
        else if (cells.get(q) === color && !seen.has(q)) {
          seen.add(q); stack.push(q);
        }
      }
    }
    groups.push({ color, stones: stones.sort(), liberties: [...liberties].sort(), count: liberties.size });
  }
  return groups;
}
